seo.metaTitle: Hashtag Generator: A Balanced Set, Not Thirty Random Tags
seo.metaDescription: Enter your topic and get a hashtag set that mixes big, medium and small tags, sized to the platform you are posting on. Free, no login.

intro: Most hashtag generators hand you thirty of the biggest tags in your category and leave you to it. That is close to useless, because a post tagged #fitness sits alongside several hundred million others and is out of sight in seconds. What actually works is a mix: a couple of big tags for the brief burst, a set of medium ones where your post stays visible long enough to be found, and a group of small specific ones where far fewer people are looking but the ones who are actually care. This free hashtag generator builds that mix for you, sized to the platform you are posting on, and it explains what each group is for so you can judge it rather than trust it.
howto: Type what your post is about in plain words, as you would describe it to a friend. Not keywords, just the sentence.
Check the topic it picked. It works this out from your words and tells you which one it chose, so if it guessed wrong you can change it in one tap.
Choose where you are posting. The advice underneath changes, because the platforms genuinely differ: thirty tags is normal on Instagram and looks like spam on X.
Set how many you want. The slider will not let you go past what the platform allows, and fewer good tags usually beats more weak ones.
Press Build. Tap any hashtag you do not like to drop it, then copy the whole set or just one group.
benefits: The three groups are the point, and they are labelled in plain language rather than as tiers or difficulty scores. Big hashtags are described as what they are: huge audiences where you disappear in seconds. Small ones are described as fewer people but the right ones. Once someone reads that once, they understand why a set of thirty enormous tags never worked, and they can build sets themselves afterwards. A tool that teaches you the rule is worth more than one that hides it.

It also builds tags from your own words, not just from a stored list. A post about banana bread gets tags from the category and tags made from the phrase itself, which is what makes the set specific to your post rather than generic to your niche. And because everything is tappable, the output is a starting point you edit rather than a block you copy blindly. Try a different set reshuffles without changing your settings, so you can look at three or four options in a few seconds.
useCases: Small accounts and new businesses get the most from this, because the broad-only approach hurts them the most and the balanced mix is exactly what they are usually missing. Anyone posting regularly uses it to avoid repeating the same block of tags on every post, which platforms notice and which stops working quickly.

It is equally useful for people who manage several accounts in different niches and cannot hold twenty categories in their head, and for anyone moving a post between platforms, since the same caption needs a very different number of tags on Instagram and on LinkedIn. Before you publish, our [hashtag counter](/tools/hashtag-counter/) checks the finished caption against the platform limits, and the [caption formatter](/tools/caption-formatter/) fixes the line breaks.

faqs.q: Does this show how many posts use each hashtag?
faqs.a: No, and no free tool can do that honestly any more. The platforms stopped offering post counts publicly, so anything claiming to show live numbers is scraping and will break, usually without telling you. What this does instead is apply the structure that makes a set work, which is the part most people get wrong regardless of the numbers.

faqs.q: How many hashtags should I actually use?
faqs.a: It depends on the platform, and the advice updates as you switch. Instagram allows thirty but most accounts do better with eight to fifteen chosen carefully. On X, one or two beat more. On LinkedIn, three to five at the end of the post. On TikTok, three to six.

faqs.q: Why mix big and small hashtags?
faqs.a: Because they do different jobs. A big tag gives you a few seconds in front of a very large audience before newer posts push you out. A small tag might only be checked by a few hundred people, but your post stays near the top of it for hours and those people chose to follow that specific subject. Small accounts get almost all their reach from the second kind.

faqs.q: Should I put hashtags in the caption or the first comment?
faqs.a: It makes no measurable difference to reach on Instagram, despite years of advice claiming otherwise. Putting them in the first comment keeps the caption clean, which is a design choice rather than a growth one. Our caption formatter can prepare either.

faqs.q: Will using the same hashtags every time hurt me?
faqs.a: It stops helping, which amounts to the same thing. Repeating an identical block looks automated and narrows you to the same audience every post. Use Try a different set between posts and swap the small tags to match what each post is actually about.
